gloss_terse: Gezer — a fortified Canaanite city on the Ephraim-Judah border, later an Israelite Levitical city
gloss_readable: Gezer was a strategically vital Canaanite city perched on the boundary between the coastal Shephelah and the hill country of Ephraim. Its king fell to Joshua at Lachish (Josh 10:33), yet Israel could not fully drive out its Canaanite inhabitants for centuries (Josh 16:10; Judg 1:29). Pharaoh eventually conquered and burned the city, handing it as a dowry to Solomon's Egyptian wife (1 Kgs 9:16–17). Assigned as a Levitical city (Josh 21:21), Gezer witnessed both David's victories over the Philistines (2 Sam 5:25; 1 Chr 14:16) and Solomon's ambitious building campaigns.

senses.1: The fortified city-state of Gezer (Tell Jezer), situated on the road between Joppa and Jerusalem, controlling a key pass from the coastal plain into the highlands. Its 15 occurrences cover Joshua's conquest narratives, the Levitical city lists, David's Philistine battles, and Solomon's royal building projects. Cross-lingual glosses consistently render the toponym (eng 'Gezer/Gazer', spa 'Gezer/Guezer', deu 'Gazer/Gezer'), with only minor transliteration variation.

gloss_terse: Exile, captivity; collectively, the community of deportees carried away from their homeland
gloss_readable: A feminine noun capturing both the bitter condition of forced displacement and the people who endure it. In its abstract sense it marks the onset of captivity — Ezekiel dates his visions by 'the year of our exile' (Ezek 1:2; 33:21; 40:1), and Jeconiah's release is reckoned from his exile year (2 Kgs 25:27). In its collective sense it names the exiled community itself: 'the exiles of Judah' whom God promises to restore (Jer 24:5; 28:4; 29:22), or 'my exiles' whom the LORD declares free through Cyrus (Isa 45:13). Amos indicts Philistia and Tyre for trafficking entire exile-communities (Amos 1:6, 9).

senses.1: The state or condition of exile and captivity, and by metonymic extension the collective body of deportees. Used absolutely for the experience of banishment (2 Kgs 25:27; Ezek 1:2; 33:21), in construct chains for specific exiled groups ('exiles of Judah,' Jer 24:5; 'exiles of Cush,' Isa 20:4), and with divine suffixes for Yahweh's own displaced people (Isa 45:13). All six target languages converge on a single meaning: exile/captivity (spa 'cautividad', fra 'exil', deu 'Verbannung').

gloss_terse: Rebuke, reproof, threatening censure — especially the awe-inspiring rebuke of God
gloss_readable: Denotes a forceful verbal censure that ranges from a wise man's corrective reproof to the terrifying blast of divine wrath. In the wisdom literature, one rebuke to a discerning person outweighs a hundred blows to a fool (Prov 17:10), and the rebuke of the wise is better than the song of fools (Eccl 7:5). Far more dramatic is God's rebuke: the sea flees at it (Ps 104:7), the foundations of the world are laid bare (Ps 18:15), and warriors fall stunned before it (Ps 76:6). Isaiah envisions a day when a thousand flee at the rebuke of one (Isa 30:17).

senses.1: A stern verbal censure or threatening reproof — whether human or divine. When spoken by people, it carries the corrective force of wisdom (Prov 13:1, 8; 17:10; Eccl 7:5). When issued by God, it becomes a cosmic weapon: Yahweh's rebuke dries up seas (Isa 50:2; Ps 104:7), exposes the earth's foundations (2 Sam 22:16; Ps 18:15), and strikes warriors lifeless (Ps 76:6). Multilingual glosses uniformly reflect this dual register: eng 'rebuke/threat', spa 'reprensión/amenaza', fra 'reproche/réprimande'.

gloss_terse: Goshen — the fertile Nile Delta region where Israel sojourned, and a district in southern Judah
gloss_readable: Goshen names first and foremost the lush eastern delta of Egypt that Joseph secured for his father's family (Gen 45:10; 46:28–34; 47:1–6). Sheltered from the plagues that struck the rest of Egypt (Exod 8:22; 9:26), it became a symbol of divine protection amid judgment. A secondary Goshen appears in the southern hill country of Judah — both a district conquered by Joshua (Josh 10:41; 11:16) and a town listed among Judah's allotments (Josh 15:51). All major translations preserve the name unchanged (spa 'Gosén/Goshén', fra 'Gosen', deu 'Goschen/Goshen').

senses.1: The proper geographical name Goshen, referring primarily to the fertile Egyptian delta region where Israel settled during the sojourn (Gen 45:10; 46:28–29; 47:1–6; 50:8) and was miraculously spared from plagues (Exod 8:22; 9:26), and secondarily to a region and town in southern Judah (Josh 10:41; 11:16; 15:51). Cross-lingual glosses consistently transliterate the toponym with minimal variation, reflecting its universal recognition as a biblical place name.

gloss_terse: Fish (collective feminine noun) — aquatic creatures as a class, especially of the sea and Nile
gloss_readable: This feminine collective noun for fish stands alongside the more common masculine דָּג, but carries a distinctly collective, class-wide force. It appears at the very outset of Scripture when God grants humanity dominion over 'the fish of the sea' (Gen 1:26, 28). It surfaces again in the Exodus plagues when the Nile's fish die (Exod 7:18, 21), in Israel's nostalgic memory of Egyptian fish eaten freely (Num 11:5), and in Ezekiel's eschatological river whose waters teem with fish 'of many kinds' (Ezek 47:9–10). Deuteronomy's prohibition against fish-shaped idols (Deut 4:18) shows how theologically charged even this humble word could become.

senses.1: Feminine collective noun for fish as a zoological class of aquatic creatures, distinguished from the masculine דָּג which may denote individual fish. Used in the creation mandate (Gen 1:26, 28), the Nile plague (Exod 7:18, 21), the nostalgic food memory of Egypt (Num 11:5), the prohibition of fish idols (Deut 4:18), and Ezekiel's eschatological river (Ezek 47:9–10). All target languages render it straightforwardly: eng 'fish', spa 'pez/pescado', fra 'poisson', deu 'Fisch'.

gloss_terse: Darius — the Persian royal name borne by Darius Hystaspis and 'Darius the Mede' in Scripture
gloss_readable: The Hebrew form דָּרְיָוֶשׁ renders the Old Persian name Dārayavauš ('he who holds firm the good'). In Ezra it identifies Darius I Hystaspis, under whose decree the Jerusalem temple was completed (Ezra 4:24; 5:5–7; 6:1, 12–15). In Daniel it names the enigmatic 'Darius the Mede' who receives the kingdom after Belshazzar's fall (Dan 5:31; 6:1–28). Haggai and Zechariah date their prophecies to 'the second year of Darius' (Hag 1:1; Zech 1:1). European translations consistently use 'Darius/Darío,' while some transliterations stay closer to the Hebrew form (eng 'Daryavesh').

senses.1: The royal Persian name Darius (דָּרְיָוֶשׁ), from Old Persian Dārayavauš, designating at least two figures: Darius I Hystaspis under whom the Second Temple was rebuilt (Ezra 4:24; 6:1, 12–15; Hag 1:1; Zech 1:1), and the mysterious 'Darius the Mede' of Daniel (Dan 6:1, 6, 9, 25, 28). Cross-lingual glosses range from close transliterations (eng 'Daryavesh') to conventional Europeanizations (spa 'Darío', fra/deu 'Darius').

gloss_terse: This; which, who — an archaic poetic pronoun serving as both demonstrative and relative
gloss_readable: An indeclinable archaic pronoun found almost exclusively in poetry, especially the Psalms and the Song of the Sea (Exod 15). As a demonstrative it means 'this' (Hab 1:11 'this his strength'; Ps 62:11 'these two things I have heard'). As a relative pronoun it parallels the more common אֲשֶׁר, introducing clauses like 'the people which you redeemed' (Exod 15:13, 16) and 'against whom we sinned' (Isa 42:24). Its haunting, elevated register gives passages an archaic solemnity that later Hebrew reserved for liturgical and prophetic contexts.

senses.1: An archaic, indeclinable pronoun functioning both demonstratively ('this') and relatively ('which, who, whom') in poetic and liturgical Hebrew. As a demonstrative: Hab 1:11 'this his strength', Ps 62:11 'these two things'. As a relative: Exod 15:13 'the people which you redeemed', Isa 42:24 'against whom we sinned', Ps 9:15 'the net which they hid'. Cross-lingual evidence reflects this duality — spa 'esta/contra quien', fra 'ce/ceci', deu 'dies/der' — confirming the single pronoun's two syntactic roles.

gloss_terse: Hur — a personal name borne by Moses' companion, a Judahite ancestor of Bezalel, and others
gloss_readable: The name Hur (חוּר, possibly meaning 'white' or 'noble') belongs to several figures, most memorably the man who, alongside Aaron, held up Moses' weary hands during the battle against Amalek at Rephidim (Exod 17:10, 12) and was left in charge when Moses ascended Sinai (Exod 24:14). A Judahite named Hur was the grandfather of Bezalel, the master craftsman of the tabernacle (Exod 31:2; 35:30; 38:22; 1 Chr 2:19–20). Other bearers include a Midianite king slain by Israel (Num 31:8; Josh 13:21) and a post-exilic leader who repaired Jerusalem's wall (Neh 3:9).

senses.1: The masculine proper name Hur (חוּר), borne by multiple biblical figures: (a) the companion of Moses and Aaron who supported Moses' hands at Rephidim (Exod 17:10, 12; 24:14), (b) the Judahite grandfather of the tabernacle craftsman Bezalel (Exod 31:2; 35:30; 1 Chr 2:19–20, 50; 4:1, 4), (c) a king of Midian killed alongside Balaam (Num 31:8; Josh 13:21), and (d) a post-exilic official (Neh 3:9; 1 Kgs 4:8). Cross-lingual forms vary slightly between 'Hur' (eng/fra/deu) and 'Jur' (spa).

gloss_terse: Hashabiah — 'Yahweh has reckoned'; a Levitical name borne by musicians, officers, and officials
gloss_readable: A theophoric name meaning 'Yahweh has taken account' or 'the LORD has reckoned,' borne by at least seven distinct individuals — all of them Levites or temple officials. David's temple musician Hashabiah served in the twenty-fifth division (1 Chr 25:3, 19). Another Hashabiah administered the tribe of Levi under David (1 Chr 27:17), and yet another oversaw affairs in Hebron (1 Chr 26:30). In the post-exilic period the name proliferates among those who returned with Ezra (Ezra 8:19, 24), sealed the covenant with Nehemiah (Neh 10:11), and served in the restored temple (Neh 11:15, 22; 12:24).

senses.1: The masculine proper name Hashabiah (חֲשַׁבְיָה / חֲשַׁבְיָהוּ), a theophoric compound meaning 'Yah(u) has reckoned,' designating multiple Levites across Israel's history: temple musicians under David (1 Chr 25:3, 19), tribal and regional officers (1 Chr 26:30; 27:17), Josiah-era Levites (2 Chr 35:9), and numerous post-exilic officials under Ezra and Nehemiah (Ezra 8:19, 24; Neh 10:11; 11:15, 22; 12:24). Cross-lingual renderings vary from close transliterations (eng 'Hashabiah/Chashavyah') to Europeanized forms (deu 'Haschabja', spa 'Hasabías/Jasabías').

gloss_terse: Purification, ritual cleansing — the prescribed process of restoring ceremonial purity
gloss_readable: A feminine noun at the heart of Israel's purity system, denoting the formal process by which a person or object is restored to a state of ritual cleanness before God. After childbirth a woman observes 'days of her purification' — thirty-three for a son, sixty-six for a daughter (Lev 12:4–6). A healed leper undergoes an elaborate cleansing rite (Lev 14:2, 23, 32), and a Nazirite defiled by sudden death must begin purification anew (Num 6:9). Ezekiel requires seven days of purification for priests after contact with the dead (Ezek 44:26), and Nehemiah celebrates that the Levites kept 'the charge of purification' (Neh 12:45).

senses.1: The process or state of ritual purification and ceremonial cleansing, used across the Levitical purity laws. Covers purification after childbirth (Lev 12:4–6), cleansing of skin disease (Lev 13:7, 35; 14:2, 23, 32), restoration after bodily discharge (Lev 15:13), Nazirite re-consecration (Num 6:9), priestly cleansing from corpse contamination (Ezek 44:26), and the general charge of maintaining temple purity (1 Chr 23:28; Neh 12:45). All target languages reflect the core meaning: spa 'purificación', fra 'purification', eng 'purification/cleansing'.
